planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past last frost; Worthmore's upright, non-vining habit and early set make it a good choice for a quick first planting with a follow-up sowing a month later.

directions: Worthmore is a University of Georgia pinkeye-type release bred from Mississippi Silver and Pinkeye Purple Hull stock, combining the parent varieties' flavor with sturdier disease tolerance. Plants grow upright with little vining, setting pods that mature to a deep purple at the green-shell stage, each holding around sixteen light tan peas with a greenish-tan eye. It shows useful field resistance to several common mosaic viruses that trouble southern peas in humid climates, making it a reliable choice where virus pressure has been a problem. Harvest at the green-shell stage for the classic fresh Southern pea pot, or let pods dry fully for storage peas.
sources: Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America (cucurbit.info)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm; the bush habit and concentrated pod set make Queen Anne well suited to a single large harvest for freezing or canning rather than a long trickle crop.

directions: Queen Anne is a true bush-type blackeye pea with no runners at all, holding its pods bunched up at foliage level where they are easy to spot and pick. It sets its crop early and all at once, which suits growers who want one concentrated harvest rather than a plant that trickles peas over many weeks. The seed itself closely resembles California Blackeye 5 but runs a bit smaller, with the same creamy flavor Gulf Coast cooks expect from a classic blackeye pea. Its compact, non-sprawling frame also makes it a practical pick for raised beds or smaller garden rows where space is tight.
sources: Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America (cucurbit.info)

planting.note: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed; Floricream's determinate, top-bearing habit concentrates pods for an efficient once-over hand or machine harvest.

directions: Floricream was developed at the University of Florida as an all-purpose cream-seeded southern pea, bred from Mississippi 32, Korean Crowder, Running Acre, and Tavares lines. It grows as a determinate, top-bearing semi-crowder type with long pods around eight inches, and the creamy-white peas carry a light brown eye and classic smooth, buttery flavor. The plant shows useful field resistance to scab and fusarium wilt, both persistent problems for southern peas in hot, humid gardens, and its concentrated fruit set makes it well suited to mechanical harvesting as well as home garden picking. It remains a solid choice for Gulf Coast growers wanting a dependable cream pea with some built-in disease tolerance.
sources: Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America (cucurbit.info)

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil; where root-knot nematodes have limited other southern peas, Charleston Nemagreen is one of the few cream-type options bred specifically to shrug off that pressure.

directions: Charleston Nemagreen was bred by USDA-ARS at Charleston, South Carolina as a root-knot nematode resistant successor to the older cream-type cultivar Bettergreen, carrying the Rk resistance gene effective against southern, Javanese, and northern root-knot nematode species. It shares the green-cotyledon trait of its cream-pea relatives, meaning pods can be left to reach the dry stage without the peas losing their fresh green color, a trait valued by home freezers and commercial processors alike. Plant habit and maturity closely track Bettergreen, so gardeners familiar with that variety will find Nemagreen behaves similarly in the row. It is a strong pick for gardens with a known history of root-knot nematode damage in legumes.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is warm; let a portion of the crop dry fully on the vine to see the green-cotyledon trait that keeps the dried peas looking freshly shelled.

directions: Bettergreen was developed by the USDA Vegetable Laboratory in Charleston, South Carolina from a single mutant plant found in a Carolina Cream planting, and became the first pinkeye-type southern pea with the green-cotyledon trait. That trait lets the peas be harvested at full dry maturity without fading from green to the usual tan or brown, a quality that frozen-food processors and home gardeners both prize for appearance. The plant also carries useful tolerance or resistance to cowpea curculio, cercospora leaf spot, southern blight, rust, and powdery mildew, giving it a sturdier disease profile than many older pinkeye varieties. It is a good option for Gulf Coast gardeners who want the classic pinkeye flavor along with broader pest and disease tolerance.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil; this pinkeye type can be left on the plant until pods near the dry stage without the peas losing their fresh green look, simplifying harvest timing.

directions: Charleston Greenpack is a pinkeye-type southern pea from the USDA Vegetable Laboratory in Charleston, South Carolina, bred to combine the green-cotyledon trait with pinkeye flavor and yields comparable to established varieties like Coronet. Peas harvested near the dry stage keep a light olive color in both seed coat and cotyledon rather than fading to tan, so dried or near-dry harvests still look freshly shelled. The plant shows excellent field resistance to blackeye cowpea mosaic virus, a major disease problem for southern peas across the region, which helps keep plantings productive through a long hot summer. It suits gardeners who want pinkeye flavor with extra insurance against virus losses.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed; because this type holds its green color through full dry maturity, pods can be left on the plant longer before shelling without sacrificing appearance.

directions: ZipperCream-GC was bred at the USDA Vegetable Laboratory in Charleston, South Carolina by crossing the green-cotyledon trait into a Zipper Cream genetic background, producing a large-seeded cream pea that keeps its fresh green color even when harvested fully dry. It was developed for growers using axial-flow combines, which require dry-stage harvest, so that the finished peas would not suffer the dulled color that dry-harvested cream peas usually show. Home gardeners benefit from the same trait by having more flexibility in harvest timing without the peas turning tan on the vine. Flavor and easy-shelling pod habit follow the familiar Zipper Cream type, making this a practical upgrade for anyone who already grows that classic variety.
sources: Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America (cucurbit.info)
